content: The Birth Cohort study identified a significant relationship between changes in conditional weight from age 11 to adulthood and elevated total cholesterol levels in adulthood. Regarding height, two studies presented conflicting results: one demonstrated an association between childhood height and adult cholesterol levels, while the other found no such association. A significant correlation was observed between waist circumference and the sum of skinfolds at age 9 with increased total cholesterol levels in adulthood. The Bogalusa Heart Study reported a positive correlation between childhood triceps skinfold thickness and adult total cholesterol levels. However, the Northern Finland Birth Cohort of 1966 found no association between the age of adiposity rebound and higher total cholesterol levels in adulthood. Thirteen studies examined the relationship between childhood and adolescent anthropometric measures and triglyceride levels in adulthood. These measures included body mass index (BMI), weight, height, waist circumference, skinfold thickness, and age at adiposity rebound. Positive associations between childhood and adolescent BMI and adult triglyceride levels were reported in studies from the Ternuzian Birth Cohort, Bogalusa Heart Study, and 1958 British Birth Cohort. Conversely, no association was observed between infant BMI and triglyceride levels in adolescence and adulthood in the Vulnerable Windows Cohort Study and the Northern Finland Birth Cohort of 1966. The Newcastle Thousand Families Cohort Study found an inverse relationship between childhood BMI and adult triglyceride levels. Rapid increases in childhood BMI were significantly associated with higher odds of developing elevated triglyceride levels in adolescence and adulthood, as reported by the Minneapolis Children’s Blood Pressure Study and ALSPAC. The Bogalusa Heart Study also demonstrated a significant association between adolescent weight status, BMI changes, and adult triglyceride levels. The Northern Finland Birth Cohort of 1966 and the New Delhi Birth Cohort Study reported that individuals with a BMI percentile >90th to <95th and changes in conditional BMI from age 2 to adulthood had an increased risk of elevated triglyceride levels in adulthood. Weight during infancy, childhood, and adolescence was also examined for its association with adult triglyceride levels. No association was found between infant weight and adult triglyceride levels in the Vulnerable Windows Cohort Study. However, the Minneapolis Children’s Blood Pressure Study reported a significant association between childhood weight and the rate of weight increase with adult triglyceride levels. The New Delhi Birth Cohort Study found a significant association between conditional weight from birth to adulthood and adult triglyceride levels. Regarding height, no association was found between infant height and adult triglyceride levels in the Vulnerable Windows Cohort Study. Similarly, individuals with peak height velocity >8 cm/year during infancy did not exhibit an increased risk of elevated triglyceride levels in adulthood. However, the Minneapolis Children’s Blood Pressure Study reported a significant positive association between childhood height and adult triglyceride levels. Rapid increases in childhood waist circumference were significantly associated with higher odds of developing elevated triglyceride levels in adolescence, as reported by ALSPAC and NHLBI studies. The sum of skinfold thickness in childhood was not significantly associated with adolescent triglyceride levels in the NHLBI study. However, a positive correlation was found between skinfold thickness in the age group of 2 to 17 years and triglyceride levels in adolescence. Ten studies (from six cohorts) analyzed the relationship between childhood and adolescent anthropometric measures and adult LDL cholesterol levels. These studies, all from developed countries, used statistical measures such as Spearman’s correlation coefficient, standard regression coefficient, percentage change, and odds ratio. Seven studies from five cohorts reported an association between childhood and adolescent BMI and adult LDL levels. Reports from the Bogalusa Heart Study and the Minneapolis Children’s Blood Pressure Study demonstrated a significant positive relationship between childhood and adolescent BMI levels and adult LDL levels. The Newcastle Thousand Families Cohort Study reported an inverse relationship between childhood BMI and adult LDL levels. BMI at adiposity rebound was not associated with adult LDL levels when adjusted for socioeconomic status, maternal age, height, weight, BMI, birth weight, and gestational age. Rapid increases in BMI were associated with higher odds of developing elevated LDL levels in late adolescence, as observed in the ALSPAC study. A significant positive association was found between the rate of increase in weight and height during childhood and adult LDL levels in the Minneapolis Children’s Blood Pressure Study. Two studies reported a significant association between childhood waist circumference and rapid increases in waist circumference with the highest LDL levels during adulthood. A significant positive association was also found between childhood skinfold thickness and adolescent and adult LDL levels. Thirteen studies (from ten cohorts) analyzed the association between childhood and adolescent anthropometric measures and adult HDL cholesterol levels. These measures included height, weight, BMI, ponderal index, waist circumference, skinfold thickness, and BMI at adiposity rebound. Studies from the Ternuzian Birth Cohort, Minneapolis Children’s Blood Pressure Study, and ALSPAC reported a negative correlation between rapid increases in BMI from ages 2 to 18 and adult HDL levels. Reports from the Bogalusa Heart Study demonstrated an inverse association between childhood BMI levels and adult HDL levels, with the association persisting after adjustment for race, age, and sex. The Northern Finland Birth Cohort Study reported no significant association between childhood BMI and adult HDL levels. A weak inverse relationship in females and a weak positive relationship in males were observed between childhood BMI and adult HDL levels when adjusted for BMI at age 50. Changes in conditional BMI from age 11 to adulthood were significantly associated with lower adult HDL levels. The Northern Finland Birth Cohort of 1966 reported no association between adiposity rebound in childhood and adult HDL levels. The 1958 British Birth Cohort reported a negative association between changes in BMI from ages 7 to 16 and adult HDL levels. Four studies examined the impact of childhood weight on adult HDL levels. The New Delhi Birth Cohort observed a significant association between changes in conditional weight from age 11 to adulthood and lower adult HDL levels. A significant negative association between childhood weight, the rate of weight increase, and adult HDL levels was observed in the Minneapolis Children’s Blood Pressure Study. The Vulnerable Windows Cohort found an association between weight increases from ages 2 to 11 and lower HDL levels at age 11. Three studies examined the relationship between height and adult HDL levels. The Vulnerable Windows Cohort found no association between birth height and HDL levels at age 11. However, the Minneapolis Children’s Blood Pressure Study reported a significant negative association between childhood height and adult HDL levels, with no association observed with the rate of height increase during childhood and adolescence. Subjects with peak height velocity >8 cm/year did not exhibit an increased risk of developing lower HDL levels in adulthood. Two studies examined the impact of childhood waist circumference on adult HDL levels. The ALSPAC and NHLBI studies reported that rapid increases in waist circumference during childhood were associated with higher odds of developing low HDL levels in adolescence. Childhood triceps skinfold thickness was negatively correlated with adult HDL levels when adjusted for race, age, and sex. The NHLBI study found a significant association between childhood skinfold thickness and decreased adult HDL levels.
